title: Aurangzeb and Dara Shikoh
hookLine: two brothers: one a pious, contested emperor, the other a mystic who studied Hindu scriptures, with a hard history between them

cards: Shah Jahan, the man who built the Taj, has sons. Two of them matter today. The elder, Dara Shikoh, is his father's favorite, a scholar who keeps company with Sufis and with Hindu holy men.

The younger, Aurangzeb, is a soldier and governor, serious, devout, careful with every prayer. When their father falls ill, the brothers go to war with each other for the throne. Only one of them will live.
And long afterward, people will still argue about both brothers, and about what India would have been if the other had won. Today: Aurangzeb and Dara Shikoh.

teach.h: DARA: WHERE THE TWO SEAS MEET.
teach.b: Dara Shikoh followed the Qadiri Sufi path. He believed that seekers in different traditions were reaching toward the same truth, and he went looking for it.

He worked with Hindu scholars to translate the Upanishads, Hindu scriptures, into Persian. And he wrote a short book comparing Sufi and Hindu terms, called Majma al-Bahrayn, the meeting place of the two seas.
The title comes from the Qur'an. In the story of Moses seeking a wise servant of God, Moses says, in Pickthall's translation: "I will not give up until I reach the point where the two rivers meet."
Aurangzeb won the war. Dara was captured, brought through Delhi in disgrace, and judged by scholars who said his writings had left Islam. He was put to death.
Their father spent his last years confined in the fort at Agra. That is the hard history. And Aurangzeb?
His long reign is remembered in more than one way.

teach.h: A PIOUS RULER, A CONTESTED REIGN.
teach.b: Some Muslims remember him as a deeply pious ruler, who, tradition says, copied the Qur'an and sewed prayer caps to pay for his own needs, and who sponsored a great collection of Islamic law.
Others, among them Hindus and Sikhs, remember the tax he restored on non-Muslims and the temples destroyed under his rule.
Historians still argue about how to weigh it all. Two brothers. One read across traditions looking for where the waters meet.
One held tightly to the law as he understood it.

how: Muslims remember Aurangzeb and Dara Shikoh in different ways: some honor Aurangzeb's personal piety and his sponsorship of Islamic law, some honor Dara Shikoh's Sufi search, and historians continue to debate both.

games.q: you're Dara Shikoh, a Muslim Sufi. you believe seekers in many traditions reach toward one truth. what do you do with your learning?
o: keep it private, among Sufis only.
work with Hindu scholars to translate their scriptures into Persian.
give up scholarship for the army.
games.why: he had the Upanishads translated into Persian and wrote a book on where Sufi and Hindu terms meet. scholars at his trial said his writings had left Islam.

practice: Bring to mind two people you love who see faith or life very differently; maybe one of them is you. Don't decide who's right: notice what each is holding onto, and what each is afraid of losing.
If you pray, you can pray for them both; if not, simply hold them both.

wordCard.voice: Dara Shikoh, the scholar-prince who studied with Sufis and Hindu holy men, translated the Upanishads, and was put to death by his brother Aurangzeb. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the meeting place of the two seas, from Qur'an 18:60, and the title of Dara Shikoh's book.
